title: Research methods in sociology
examples: What is the difference between a survey and an interview?
When should I use observation in my study?
Can I use these methods to prove a theory?

explain.say: Today we are looking at ways to study people and society.

items: Surveys collect data from many people.
Interviews talk to people one by one.
Observation watches people in real life.

explain.say: A survey uses written questions for many people to answer.

items: Example: Age | Example: Opinion | Example: Rating

explain.say: An interview involves talking to someone face to face or on the phone.
Observation means watching people and recording what you see happen.
In daily life, think about how a shop owner studies customers.

draw.text: Real Life: Shop owner studying shoppers.

explain.say: A common mistake is assuming people answer truthfully in surveys.

items: People might give socially desirable answers.
They might forget details when answering.
This affects the reliability of the data.

draw.text: Mistake: People might not be honest.

faq.q: How do I know if my data from a survey is good enough?
faq.a: You need a large enough and representative group of people. This helps make your findings more reliable.
asks: How big should my sample size be?

faq.q: What is the difference between an open and closed question?
faq.a: Closed questions have set answers like yes or no. Open questions ask for detailed written explanations.
asks: What if I use too many open questions?
Are open questions harder to grade?

faq.q: Is observation always ethical to use in research?
faq.a: Ethics are very important. You must get permission if people know they are being watched.
asks: Do I need permission to watch in public?
What if people feel uncomfortable being watched?

faq.q: Can I use all three methods at the same time?
faq.a: Yes, combining methods gives a richer picture. This is called triangulation in research.

faq.q: What is bias when I am observing people?
faq.a: Bias is when your own expectations influence what you record. You must remain objective to avoid this.
asks: How do I avoid my own opinions affecting my notes?

facts: Surveys are useful for gathering data from a large number of people quickly.
Interviews allow researchers to explore complex ideas in depth with one person.
Observation provides naturalistic data, showing behaviour as it naturally occurs.
Ethical considerations require informed consent from participants.

quiz.say: A researcher wants to know the general opinion of students on school uniforms across the whole school.
quiz.show: Which method is best for broad opinion?
quiz.why: Surveys are designed to collect standardized data from many people efficiently.

wrong.0: Interviews are too time-consuming for gathering general opinions from everyone.
wrong.1: Observation only shows what people do, not what they think about uniforms.
wrong.2: This only represents a very small and biased group of people.

quiz.say: A student is studying how students use the library during lunch break.
quiz.show: What method should the student use?
quiz.why: Observation allows the student to record actual behaviour without influencing it.

wrong.1: Students might not remember or accurately report their behaviour in a survey.
wrong.2: Asking students about their behaviour might make them act differently than usual.
wrong.3: Teachers might only see certain behaviours or have their own perspectives.

quiz.say: A researcher wants to understand a person's detailed feelings about moving to a new city.
quiz.show: Which method allows for deep understanding?
quiz.why: Interviews allow for follow-up questions, digging deep into complex emotions and reasons.

wrong.1: Surveys limit responses to pre-set options, missing emotional depth.
wrong.2: Observation cannot access the internal thoughts or feelings of the person.
wrong.3: News articles show public summaries, not the individual's personal feelings.
